defaults.permitted_development: Across Hampshire, agricultural buildings can benefit from Part 6 rights only where the land is a genuine agricultural unit and the proposal is reasonably necessary for agriculture. Prior approval often turns on siting, scale, design and whether the building really serves day-to-day farming rather than storage or mixed commercial use.

rules.height_rules: Across Hampshire, many Part 6 schemes have to stay within a 12m overall height limit, with tighter restrictions near safeguarded aerodromes. Ridge, eaves and roof profile still have to look proportionate to the unit they serve.
rules.depth_rules: There is no householder-style depth rule. The real question is whether the span, footprint and overall scale stay reasonably necessary for the agricultural unit rather than drifting into an oversized commercial shed.
rules.boundary_rules: Across Hampshire, the critical siting questions are usually proximity to roads, homes, protected buildings and open public views. Noise, odour, traffic and visual impact can all remove the comfort of relying on Part 6.
rules.roof_rules: Roof form is judged through height, bulk and the prior-approval context. Large reflective roofs or heavy ridges can be the feature that makes a building look excessive in the landscape.
rules.materials_rules: Use practical agricultural materials and muted colours that reduce glare and help the building sit quietly in the landscape rather than reading as industrial cladding.

rules.permitted_development: For agricultural buildings, the right question is not just whether the structure fits on the land, but whether it is truly required for an active agricultural unit. In Basingstoke and Deane, the planning case is strongest where the building reads as ordinary farm infrastructure rather than a large multipurpose shed in the countryside.

rules.boundary_rules: At the edge of the holding, the key questions are usually neighbour amenity, highway relationship, landscape exposure and any protected setting nearby. In Basingstoke and Deane, separation from homes, highway edges and public views is often the main boundary test.
